content.one_sentence_role: Restricts a set isometry and its inverse to the two contained lenses.
content.natural_language_statement: Let $E,F$ be real normed spaces, $S\subseteq E$, $T\subseteq F$, and $f:S\to T$ a bijective isometry. Choose $x,y\in S$ and $r\in\mathbb R$. Write $\Lambda_r(x,y)=\overline B(x,r)\cap\overline B(y,r)$. If $$\frac{\|x-y\|}{2}\le r,\qquad \Lambda_r(x,y)\subseteq S,\qquad \Lambda_r(f(x),f(y))\subseteq T,$$ then $f((x+y)/2)=(f(x)+f(y))/2$.
content.assumptions: The half-distance bound and both displayed lens inclusions are assumed for the same points, radius and isometry. There is no openness or convexity requirement on $S,T$.
content.conclusion: The midpoint belongs to $S$ and its image is the midpoint of the two images. The target half-distance bound is a consequence of distance preservation.
content.proof_summary: Use both inclusions to restrict the forward and inverse maps; then apply the lens midpoint theorem to that restriction.
proof_steps: If $z\in \Lambda_r(x,y)$, then $z\in S$ and $$\|f(z)-f(x)\|=\|z-x\|\le r,\qquad\|f(z)-f(y)\|=\|z-y\|\le r.$$ Hence $f(z)$ lies in the target lens. Conversely, for $w$ in that lens, the target inclusion allows $f^{-1}(w)$ to be formed, and the same two distance identities put it in the source lens. This is precisely the bijective isometry in [Restriction to corresponding lenses](https://github.com/r-tanaka-math/mathlib-annex/blob/437e6e46228bbb8e91211ebded349d7a30020e73/MathlibAnnex/Analysis/Normed/Affine/IsometryExtension/Local.lean#L82-L118).

Distance preservation gives $\|f(x)-f(y)\|/2=\|x-y\|/2\le r$. The source half-distance bound and [Midpoint membership](https://github.com/r-tanaka-math/mathlib-annex/blob/437e6e46228bbb8e91211ebded349d7a30020e73/MathlibAnnex/Analysis/Normed/Affine/IsometryExtension/Local.lean#L34-L38) also give $(x+y)/2\in \Lambda_r(x,y)\subseteq S$.

Apply [Midpoint preservation between lenses](https://github.com/r-tanaka-math/mathlib-annex/blob/437e6e46228bbb8e91211ebded349d7a30020e73/MathlibAnnex/Analysis/Normed/Affine/IsometryExtension/Local.lean#L66-L80) to the restricted isometry, source foci $x,y$, target foci $f(x),f(y)$ and radius $r$. Both half-distance hypotheses were checked above. Since this restriction evaluates to the original $f$, its output is $f((x+y)/2)=(f(x)+f(y))/2$.
